newsitem.title: USA: CBOT to accept transgenic soy, despite protests.
newsitem.headline: CBOT to accept transgenic soy, despite protests.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade Chairman Patrick Arbor said the exchange will accept transgenic soybeans for delivery against CBOT futures contracts, despite opposition to the soybeans by some consumer and trade groups.
Following a breakfast Friday to celebrate 60 years of soybean futures trading at the CBOT, Arbor said exchange leaders are not considering any restrictions on transgenic soybeans.
Transgenic soybeans have been genetically-altered to withstand treatment by the herbicide Roundup.
Use of the transgenic soybeans has been criticized by European and U.S. consumer groups and Greenpeace.

These groups are planning demonstrations Monday in Washington and Chicago aimed at discouraging the use of these soybeans. Greenspeace distributed flyers Thursday at the CBOT opposing use of the soybeans.
Also, some of these groups want products containing transgenic soybeans or soybean products to be labeled.
Proponents of the new soybean said labeling is virtually impossible because soybean products are used in a vast array of products.

American Soybean Association President David Erickson, who attended the CBOT breakfast, said ASA supports the use of transgenic soybeans, which he said have been proven safe and are identical to conventional soybeans.
"They look like, taste like and process like soybeans because they are soybeans," he said. Erickson said he will use trangenic soybeans on his Illinois farm.

Monsanto Co, which created the Roundup-resistant technology for the soybeans, forecasts U.S. farmers will plant five million to 10 million acres of transgenic soybeans next spring up from about one million this year.
U.S. farmers are expected to harvest 63.4 million acres of soybeans this fall.
Greenpeace opposes genetic engineering calling it experimental and alleging it promotes allergies and a rising dependence on herbicides.
Monsanto spokeswoman Karen Marshall said the transgenic soybeans require less herbicides, because Roundup controls a greater variety of weeds than competing products.
